topicName: URI Design & Naming Conventions (Pluralization, Hierarchies, Query Parameters)
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"URI Design & Naming Conventions in REST APIs"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Designing clean, intuitive, and consistent Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) is a foundational skill for building robust RESTful APIs. Because URIs serve as the public interface for your application, poor design leads to brittle integrations, confusion, and maintenance overhead. This tutorial covers industry best practices for pluralization, resource hierarchies, and query parameter usage."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Resource Naming and Pluralization"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"REST APIs manage resources, which are typically represented by nouns rather than verbs. Avoid putting actions like GET, POST, or delete in your URI paths; instead, rely on HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to define the operation."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use plural nouns for collection resources (e.g., /users instead of /user)."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Use singular nouns only when referring to a specific singleton resource or configuration."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Keep URI paths lowercase and use hyphens (-) to separate compound words (kebab-case)."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"# Correct:
GET /users
GET /user-profiles/123

# Incorrect:
GET /GetUser
GET /user/123/get-profile"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Hierarchical Relationships"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"When resources have parent-child relationships, reflect this hierarchy directly within the URI path. However, avoid going deeper than two or three levels, as excessively nested URIs become difficult to read and maintain."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"# Accessing a specific post belonging to a specific user:
GET /users/42/posts/15

# Accessing all comments for that post:
GET /users/42/posts/15/comments"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Query Parameters for Filtering, Sorting, and Pagination"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"While URI paths represent specific resources and hierarchical structures, query parameters should be used to modify the behavior of requests. They are ideal for filtering collections, sorting data, and controlling pagination limits."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Pagination: Use parameters like 'limit' and 'offset' (or 'page' and 'per_page')."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Filtering: Use specific resource attributes as query parameters."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Sorting: Use a 'sort' parameter with a prefix (like minus for descending) or a separate 'direction' parameter."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"# Filtering active users, sorted by creation date descending, limited to 10 results
GET /users?status=active&sort=-created_at&limit=10&offset=0"},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Adhering to these RESTful URI design principles ensures that your API remains intuitive and scalable. Always prioritize consistency: choose a standard convention for casing, pluralization, and parameter naming, and apply it uniformly across your entire application."}]
